fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that most of the challenge isn't really about the algorithms anymore. When I started working on reinforcement learning for language, back around 2015 with text-based games, the bottleneck was that the models couldn't read. Now the models read and write extremely well, and the bottleneck has shifted almost entirely to the environment and the reward.

If you look at where RL has produced its biggest wins, whether it's games or more recently math and code, it's always been places where you have a cheap simulator and a clean signal. You can roll out millions of trajectories, you know whether you won the game or whether the unit test passed, and you can just grind. Enterprise problems have almost none of that. You can't replay a customer interaction a million times. You can't run a thousand variations of a refund flow against a real billing system. And the thing you actually care about, whether the customer left satisfied or whether the contract got processed correctly, often doesn't show up until days later, if it shows up at all.

So the first thing you end up doing is building simulators, and that turns out to be a research problem in its own right. We saw this with WebShop and later with SWE-bench. Most of the effort wasn't the agent, it was constructing an environment that was faithful enough that improvements in it transferred to the real thing. In an enterprise, that means modeling the tools, the data, the edge cases, and sometimes the humans on the other end, and every company's version of that is a little different.

The second piece is reward specification. In a game, the score is given to you. In a business, the objective is a bundle of things that are partially in tension. You want the agent to resolve the issue, but also follow policy, not overpromise, not escalate unnecessarily, and do it in a tone the company is comfortable with. If you collapse that into a single scalar carelessly, the model will find the shortcut. It will learn that the fastest way to end a conversation is to say yes to everything, or to transfer to a human. So a lot of the work is figuring out how to decompose outcomes into things you can actually verify, and being honest about what you can't.

And then the third thing, which people underestimate, is that the horizon is long and the actions are consequential. A single trajectory might be thirty tool calls, several of which have side effects in a real system. Exploration in the classic RL sense, just trying things to see what happens, is not an option when "trying things" means issuing a refund or modifying a record. So you need a lot more structure, a lot more offline data, and a much tighter loop between the people who understand the process and the people training the model.

If I had to summarize it, I'd say the challenge is that enterprise RL forces you to take seriously everything the benchmark setting lets you ignore. The models are ready. The environments and the feedback signals mostly aren't, and building them is where most of the real work is right now.

r002.rationale: It clearly states that constructing faithful environments and feedback signals requires most of the work, while the models and agent are comparatively less difficult.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest challenge is defining the reward, and closely related to that, building an environment you can actually learn in.

Look at where reinforcement learning has really worked: games like Go or Atari, and more recently math and coding. In those settings you have a crisp signal. You win or lose. The proof checks or it doesn't. The unit tests pass or they don't. And you can simulate millions of episodes cheaply. That's the ideal recipe for RL.

Enterprise problems are almost the opposite. Say an agent is handling a customer service conversation, processing an insurance claim, or doing something in a company's internal workflow. What counts as success? Partly whether the task got done. But it also has to follow the company's policies, which are often written in natural language, sometimes ambiguous, and they change over time. It has to interact with real systems and databases correctly. And the end user has to have a good experience. Those goals can pull in different directions, and the true signal, whether the customer was satisfied or the issue stayed resolved, often arrives much later, if at all. So the reward is sparse, delayed, noisy, and multi-objective all at once.

Then there's exploration. RL fundamentally learns by trying things and seeing what happens. You can't let an agent try random things on real customers or production systems. So you need a simulated environment: simulated users, mock versions of the backend tools and APIs, and some way to check the outcome. Building those environments with enough fidelity that what the agent learns actually transfers is a lot of work, and it's very domain-specific. Every enterprise has its own long tail of edge cases.

The last piece people underestimate is reliability. In a research benchmark, solving a task 70% of the time looks impressive. In an enterprise setting, the question is whether the agent handles this kind of request correctly every time, across thousands of slightly different conversations. Optimizing for that consistency, rather than average-case performance, changes how you think about evaluation and about the reward itself.

So I'm optimistic about RL here. The models are now good enough at language and reasoning that you're not starting from scratch. But the hard, unglamorous work is in the environments, the simulators, and the verifiers. Whoever gets good at building those for real business domains will unlock a lot of value.

r001.rationale: The response discusses enterprise-specific rewards, policies, systems, and edge cases, but it does not state that deep understanding of the enterprise problem is necessary to determine whether RL is appropriate.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes that environments, simulators, and verifiers require substantial work, but it does not clearly compare that effort as exceeding the work of the reinforcement-learning component itself.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the biggest challenge really comes down to the reward signal. In the classic RL success stories — games like Go or Atari, even a lot of robotics benchmarks — you have this beautifully clean, well-defined notion of success. You won the game or you didn't, you got the score or you didn't. Enterprise problems almost never look like that.

Take something like customer service, which is where I spend a lot of my time these days. What does it mean for an agent to have done a good job? It's not just "did the ticket get closed." Maybe the issue got resolved but the customer had a terrible experience. Maybe the agent followed company policy perfectly but took three times longer than it needed to. You have these multiple, often competing objectives — resolution, customer satisfaction, compliance, efficiency — and nobody hands you a scalar reward function that captures all of that. So a huge amount of the real work is actually reward design and evaluation design, which is much less glamorous than the algorithms but ends up being the bottleneck.

The second piece, which is closely related, is the environment. RL fundamentally needs the agent to try things and learn from the consequences, but in an enterprise setting you can't just let an agent loose on real customers or real production systems to explore. A mistake isn't a lost game — it's a refund issued incorrectly or a frustrated customer. So you need high-fidelity simulations of these environments, and building simulators that actually capture the messiness of real users and real business processes is genuinely hard. The gap between your simulator and reality becomes the gap in your agent's performance.

And then there's the long-horizon nature of it all. These tasks can span dozens of steps — looking things up, calling tools, going back and forth with a person — and the feedback only arrives at the very end, if at all. Credit assignment over those horizons, with sparse and noisy signals, is still an open problem. I actually find this exciting, because it means the enterprise setting isn't just an application area for RL — it's pushing on the core research questions in ways that the game benchmarks never did.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it's not the learning algorithm. That's the thing people get wrong. The algorithms we have are good enough — PPO, GRPO, whatever flavor you like. The bottleneck is everything around them.

The first problem is the reward. In all the domains where RL has worked spectacularly — games, math, competitive programming — you get the reward for free. The board tells you that you won. The unit test passes or it doesn't. Now go into an enterprise and ask, "did the agent handle this insurance claim well?" There's no function that returns a number. There's a human with fifteen years of tacit knowledge who looks at it and says, "eh, I wouldn't have phrased it that way, and you should have escalated." And when you push on why, you find out that half the criteria aren't written down anywhere, and the other half are written down in a document that's three years out of date and that nobody actually follows. So a huge fraction of the real work in deploying RL in these settings is just reward engineering — building the evaluator, the rubric, the judge. And that's a knowledge elicitation problem, not an ML problem.

The second one is that you can't explore. RL fundamentally works by trying things and failing a lot. In a simulator, failure is free. In an enterprise workflow, failure means you sent the wrong email to a customer, or you issued a refund you shouldn't have, or you modified a record in a system of record that eleven downstream processes depend on. These actions are irreversible and they have real costs. So the sample complexity story that we're all comfortable with in research — millions of episodes — just doesn't transfer. You need environments. You need faithful sandboxes of the customer's actual stack, with their actual data distributions, and building those is unglamorous, expensive engineering work that nobody writes papers about. I'd say that's where most of our effort actually goes.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated: the horizon and the credit assignment problem are genuinely brutal. A real workflow might be two hundred steps across six different systems over three days, and the outcome you care about shows up at the very end. Figuring out which of those two hundred decisions was the bad one — that's a hard problem even with a perfect reward signal at the end.

So my short answer is: the research community optimized for settings where the environment and the reward come for free, and in the enterprise, neither one does. That gap is the whole game right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses enterprise-specific reward design and tacit knowledge, but does not state that deep understanding is necessary to determine where RL is appropriate.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the bottleneck is everything around the algorithms and describes reward engineering, evaluators, sandboxes, and environments as the main work.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the main challenge is that RL needs a good environment and a good reward, and enterprises usually have neither.

In games or math problems, you know what winning looks like and you can try millions of times. In an enterprise setting, say a customer service agent handling a refund, the goal is fuzzy. You need the agent to resolve the issue and follow company policy. You need it to avoid doing something it shouldn't, and to be pleasant while doing it. That's hard to write down as a clean reward. And you can't let a half-trained agent experiment on real customers or real databases the way you'd let it explore in a simulator.

So you have to build realistic environments: simulated users, simulated tools and databases, and policies that reflect how the business works. That's a lot of effort, and if the simulator is off, the agent learns to exploit its quirks and then fails in the real world.

The second piece is reliability. In a demo, it's fine if the agent gets it right most of the time. In an enterprise, if it handles the same kind of request a hundred times, you need it to succeed all hundred. When we built benchmarks like τ-bench, what stood out was how much performance dropped when you asked whether the agent could do the same task correctly many times in a row, rather than just once. Current training methods don't optimize for that kind of consistency very well.

So the problem isn't really the RL algorithms. It's defining success, building environments you can safely learn in, and getting from "usually works" to "can be trusted."

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the biggest challenge is specifying the reward. In a research benchmark, someone has already defined the objective: win the game, pass the test, maximize the score. In an enterprise, the objective is spread across stakeholders and is often vague. A customer support workflow might be judged on resolution time, satisfaction, cost, and compliance at once, and some of those outcomes only show up weeks later. That leaves you with sparse or noisy feedback, and if you optimize a proxy too hard, the agent finds ways to hit the metric without doing what you wanted.

That ties directly into exploration. RL learns by trying things, but you can't let an agent experiment freely on a live billing system or a patient records database. So you end up training in simulators, and simulators never quite match production. That gap is where a lot of projects quietly fail.

If I had to pick one starting point, it would be being precise about what success looks like and how you'd measure it before you touch the algorithm. That's where most of the difficulty sits, upstream of the RL itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest challenge is creating an environment where the system can try things and get meaningful feedback. In a game, you can play millions of times, and you have a fairly clear signal of whether you’re doing well. In an enterprise setting, trying something might mean changing a customer’s account or making a consequential business decision. That exploration has a cost.

And then there’s the question of what you reward. Completing a task quickly isn’t necessarily the same as completing it correctly or satisfying the customer. So you need both a safe way to gather experience and a feedback signal that reflects the actual business objective. Getting those pieces right is often harder than choosing the reinforcement learning algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that reinforcement learning typically needs a lot of trial and error, and in an enterprise setting, that trial and error has a real cost. You can let an agent play a game millions of times, but you can’t necessarily let it make millions of decisions involving customers or business operations just to learn what works.

So the question becomes: can you learn from the data you already have, and improve without taking unacceptable risks? Historical data helps, but it only tells you what happened under the decisions people actually made. It doesn’t tell you what would have happened if you’d done something different. And you also need a reward that captures the business outcome you care about. Getting that feedback and making learning efficient enough to be practical is a big part of the challenge.
